summary: Defines MIB objects for configuring, monitoring and controlling routers that run the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level, and it was replaced by RFC 6527.

eli5.summary: VRRP lets a backup router take over if the main one fails. This provides the control panel.

subtitle: SNMP objects for configuring and monitoring routers that run VRRP.

tldr.problem: Networks need a way to monitor and configure routers running the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol, which provides automatic failover when a router goes down.
tldr.mechanism: Defines a management information base (MIB) with three groups of SNMP objects: operations (configuration and control), statistics (monitoring), and notifications (alerts). These objects let administrators query and manage virtual routers.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can use standard SNMP tools to see which router is the master, monitor failover events, and adjust redundancy settings. This RFC was superseded by RFC 6527.

today: RFC 2787 is now Historic, superseded by RFC 6527 (published 2012) which adds support for IPv6 and updates the MIB structure. The newer RFC is the standards-track specification for VRRP management.

sections.title: Introduction to VRRP Management
sections.content:
The Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) allows multiple physical routers to act as one virtual router, so if the primary fails, a backup takes over automatically. Network administrators need a way to monitor which router is the master, check how many times failover has happened, and configure redundancy parameters like priority and advertisement intervals.

This RFC extends the SNMP management framework with a MIB (Management Information Base) containing objects for VRRP routers, allowing administrators to manage them using standard SNMP tools like network monitoring systems.
sections.eli5: When a main router fails, a backup instantly takes over so traffic keeps flowing. This is the control panel where you can see what is happening and change the settings.

sections.title: VRRP and MIB Structure
sections.content:
In VRRP, a single physical router can run multiple instances of virtual routers. Each virtual router is identified by a combination of an interface index (ifIndex) and a Virtual Router ID (VRID, 1 to 255). Each virtual router has an associated set of one or more IP addresses that it protects.

The VRRP MIB is organized into three conformance groups. The vrrpOperations group contains objects for configuration, such as priority, authentication type, and advertisement interval. The vrrpStatistics group contains counters and events. The vrrpNotifications group defines SNMP traps (alerts) for state changes and errors.
sections.eli5: One physical router can pretend to be many virtual routers. Each one has an ID number. You can look up each one and see its status, change its settings, and get alerts when something changes.

sections.title: The Operations Table
sections.content:
The core of the VRRP MIB is the vrrpOperTable, which has one row per virtual router instance. Key objects in this table include:

vrrpOperState: the current state (initialize, backup, or master).

vrrpOperPriority: a number from 0 to 255 determining which router becomes master. A priority of 255 means this router owns the IP address natively. A priority of 0 from the master signals that the master is leaving.

vrrpOperAdvertisementInterval: seconds between keepalive messages from the master. The default is 1 second.

vrrpOperPreemptMode: whether a higher-priority router can take over from a lower-priority master.

A second table, vrrpAssoIpAddrTable, lists the IP addresses protected by each virtual router.
sections.eli5: A table shows each virtual router, who is in charge, how often it says "I am alive," and whether a better router can take over. Another table says which IP addresses each virtual router protects.

sections.title: Configuration and Control Objects
sections.content:
Administrators can read and write several operational parameters. The vrrpOperAdminState object enables or disables a virtual router. It must be set to down before modifying other read-create objects.

The vrrpOperAuthType specifies how VRRP advertisements are authenticated: no authentication, simple text password, or IP authentication header. The vrrpOperAuthKey holds the authentication key (up to 16 octets; when read, it always returns empty for security).

The vrrpOperVirtualMacAddr is derived from the VRID and is used by the virtual router for ARP replies and packet transmission. When a virtual router transitions to master state, it uses this MAC address.

The vrrpOperRowStatus object controls whether the row is active, allowing addition and removal of virtual routers through SNMP.
sections.eli5: You can turn a virtual router on or off, set a password, pick a priority number, and decide whether to use authentication. You can even add or remove virtual routers.

sections.title: Statistics and Monitoring
sections.content:
The vrrpStatistics group provides counters and timestamps for monitoring. The vrrpRouterStatsTable contains statistics per virtual router, such as the number of advertisements received, advertisements sent, protocol errors, and IP address owner transitions (master transitions when the actual owner of an IP is detected).

The vrrpOperVirtualRouterUpTime object tracks when the virtual router transitioned out of the initialize state. Administrators use these statistics to detect flapping (frequent transitions), authentication failures, and other problems.

The vrrpNotifications group defines SNMP traps for events like state transitions and protocol errors, allowing management stations to be alerted in real time.
sections.eli5: You can count how many times each virtual router switched roles, how many errors happened, and how long it has been running. You can also set up alerts to go off when something important happens.
